papers.relied_on: Row 8 relied on the abstract for consensus that stimulated C-peptide is the appropriate primary outcome in T1D beta-cell preservation trials (row 8 D2 3, D8 3).
papers.full_text_shows: The text was extracted from a two-column PDF, so lines interleave and the beta symbol is lost, but the content is readable. It gives the DCCT-based rationale: stimulated C-peptide of 0.2 nmol/l or more was linked to lower retinopathy, nephropathy and hypoglycaemia, and it advises testing between 70 and 200 mg/dl. The workshop sets out the outcome for trials, not a routine-care test.
papers.quote: C-peptide is considered to be a good marker of insulin secretion
papers.key_numbers: Stimulated C-peptide threshold 0.2 nmol/l (DCCT intensive group); test glucose window 70-200 mg/dl; MMTT 2-h peak usually before 90 min
papers.role_in_work: Consensus source for row 8 surrogate acceptance
papers.design: ADA workshop report (expert consensus with literature and DCCT data review)
papers.population_and_size: DCCT-derived data and recent-onset T1D trial candidates; no single sample size
papers.assay_or_platform: Not a single assay; assay variability discussed generally
papers.quality_note: Consensus from a 2001 meeting, over 20 years old; adoption by a guideline body not stated in the passages read; sponsor and conflict details not checked.

papers.relied_on: Row 8 relied on the abstract for MMTT being preferred over the glucagon stimulation test for trials (D2 3, D8 3, D4 2).
papers.full_text_shows: Confirms two parallel studies (TrialNet and ECPT) showing MMTT is more sensitive, more reproducible and better tolerated; nausea occurred in 75-81% of glucagon tests. It also states that fasting C-peptide correlates r=0.95 and 0.93 with MMTT AUC and that a stimulated test may not add benefit in clinical practice beyond fasting or random C-peptide. It says DCCT linked stimulated, not fasting, C-peptide to outcomes, and that no formal study compares them.
papers.quote: Any stimulated test is expensive and time consuming and thus may not provide benefits in clinical practice beyond a fasting or a random C-peptide measurement.
papers.key_numbers: MMTT vs fasting r 0.95/0.93; GST nausea 75-81%, vomiting 5-11%; MMTT peak about 88 min, GST peak about 6 min; fasting duplicate r about 0.90
papers.role_in_work: Source for MMTT protocol choice and endpoint reliability in row 8
papers.design: Two parallel analyses of repeated tests in trial cohorts (TrialNet, ECPT)
papers.population_and_size: Recent-onset T1D, age 8-35 years, duration 3 months-3 years; sample sizes not re-read (earlier project note: n=148 TrialNet, 118 ECPT)
papers.measure_type: C-peptide, stimulated (mixed-meal vs glucagon); fasting C-peptide compared
papers.assay_or_platform: Trial laboratory C-peptide assay (platform not captured in the passages read)
papers.quality_note: Standardized trial conditions; not routine-care data; sensitivity analysis excluded glucose outside 70-200 mg/dl.

papers.relied_on: Row 8 cited the albiglutide RCT as an example of MMTT 2-h C-peptide AUC used as a primary endpoint.
papers.full_text_shows: Phase 2 trial, 67 randomized (50 albiglutide, 17 placebo), primary endpoint MMTT 2-h C-peptide AUC change at week 52. Mean change was -0.16 nmol/L placebo vs -0.13 albiglutide (P=0.65 non-Bayesian); the study was stopped early and funded by GSK, and the Bayesian posterior difference was 0.12 nmol/L (0-0.24). It is a negative trial; it supports endpoint use, not that C-peptide guides care.
papers.quote: no significant secondary endpoint differences were noted
papers.key_numbers: n=67 (50:17); completers 40/50 and 12/17; change -0.13 vs -0.16 nmol/L; P=0.6505; posterior difference 0.12 (0-0.24); P(diff >=0.2)=0.097
papers.role_in_work: Example of the endpoint in an RCT
papers.design: Randomized, placebo-controlled phase 2, 52 weeks, Bayesian primary analysis using prior placebo data
papers.population_and_size: Adults with newly diagnosed T1D (within 8 weeks), 67 randomized
papers.quality_note: Industry-funded (GSK authors), stopped early, small, negative; relies on a Bayesian prior.

papers.relied_on: Row 9 relied on the abstract for misclassification of type 3c diabetes as type 2 (87.8%) and need for insulin.
papers.full_text_shows: Primary-care record study in England (2,360,631 people, 31,789 new adult-onset diabetes cases, 559 after pancreatic disease). The word C-peptide does not appear in the text; no insulin or C-peptide measurement was used. Its value for row 9 is the misclassification rate and insulin need, not the test.
papers.quote: Diabetes of the exocrine pancreas is frequently labeled type 2
papers.key_numbers: Incidence after pancreatic disease 2.59 per 100,000 person-years vs 1.64 for type 1; 87.8% labelled type 2; 2.7% labelled exocrine; insulin within 5 years 4.1% (T2D), 20.9% (after acute pancreatitis), 45.8% (chronic pancreatic disease); poor control aOR 1.7
papers.role_in_work: Burden and misclassification context for row 9
papers.design: Retrospective cohort, UK primary care database (2005-2016)
papers.population_and_size: Adults with new-onset diabetes, n=31,789; 559 with preceding pancreatic disease
papers.measure_type: None (no insulin or C-peptide measure); coded diagnosis, HbA1c and insulin use only
papers.quality_note: Coding-based, UK; misclassification and selection bias acknowledged by the authors; does not test C-peptide.

papers.relied_on: Row 9 relied on the abstract for lower C-peptide in pancreatogenic diabetes versus T2D (D2 1, D8 1).
papers.full_text_shows: Single-centre cross-sectional study, 44 pancreatogenic (26 cancer, 18 chronic pancreatitis) vs 35 T2D. The measure was fasting C-peptide, 0.81 vs 1.71 nmol/L (P<0.001). C-peptide did not enter the cut-off table; fasting insulin did (below 85 pmol/L: sensitivity 75.0%, specificity 82.9%), and the composite index (below 2.40) reached 84.1% and 80.0%. Authors flag low statistical power and small size.
papers.quote: We found significantly lower insulin and C-peptide levels in patients with pancreatogenic diabetes.
papers.key_numbers: Fasting C-peptide 0.81 vs 1.71 nmol/L; insulin cut-off <85 pmol/L sens 75.0 spec 82.9 OR 14.50; type 3c index <2.40 sens 84.1 spec 80.0; BMI <24.65 sens 50.0 spec 97.1
papers.role_in_work: Only retrieved comparison of C-peptide in type 3c vs T2D
papers.population_and_size: New-onset or short-duration (up to 6 months) diabetes; n=79
papers.measure_type: Fasting-based insulin and C-peptide (with HOMA-IR); no stimulated test
papers.assay_or_platform: C-peptide platform not captured in the passages read; adiponectin by ELISA (BioVendor)
papers.quality_note: Small, single-centre, several tests under-powered; no external validation; mixes pancreatic cancer and chronic pancreatitis.

papers.full_text_shows: Single case: glucose 668 mg/dL, HbA1c 19%, C-peptide 0.87 ng/mL (reference 1.1-4.4). Serum insulin was drawn after exogenous insulin and so was not interpretable. C-peptide is used as supportive evidence next to history; no cut-off or stimulated test.
papers.quote: low C-peptide levels suggestive of impaired endogenous insulin secretion
papers.key_numbers: C-peptide 0.87 ng/mL (ref 1.1-4.4); glucose 668 mg/dL; HbA1c 19.0%; insulin 9.4 uIU/mL drawn on exogenous insulin
papers.measure_type: C-peptide, random (single sample); insulin not interpretable
papers.quality_note: Anecdotal, no evidence on decision change.

proposals.reason: Full text says fasting C-peptide correlates r=0.95 and 0.93 with MMTT AUC and that no study shows the stimulated value is more meaningful per subject; the workshop case rests on DCCT stimulated data. Alternatives (fasting C-peptide) are closer than 'clearly adds'. Clarification 19 needs data showing the measure changes the answer given the alternatives.
proposals.quote: Without a formal study using a fasting or random C-peptide value in addition to a stimulated test, it is not possible to determine which is more clinically meaningful

proposals.reason: C116 full text confirms a single-centre case-control with fasting C-peptide only; no change. C049 has no C-peptide.
proposals.quote: We found significantly lower insulin and C-peptide levels in patients with pancreatogenic diabetes.

proposals.reason: Consensus plus randomized comparison confirmed; the negative albiglutide trial does not change surrogate acceptance.
proposals.quote: no significant secondary endpoint differences were noted

claim_issues.issue: Add that Greenbaum 2008 full text reports fasting C-peptide correlating r=0.95/0.93 with MMTT AUC and says a stimulated test may add nothing in clinical practice; and that the albiglutide trial was negative, stopped early and GSK-funded.
Woodmansey 2017 contains no insulin or C-peptide measurement (word absent); it supports misclassification (87.8%) and insulin need only. Do not cite it for the C-peptide test itself.

The only C-peptide data (Juza 2025) are fasting; 'fasting or MMTT-stimulated' is not supported by this source for the type 3c vs T2D question. Its cut-off table has insulin (<85 pmol/L), not C-peptide.
